---
title: Feature flags
description: Flag policy, lifecycle catalog, admin dashboard and the mobile evaluation contract.
---

The root `config/feature-flags.json` owns the mobile runtime flag inventory. Each
array entry has
`key` (unique snake_case), `description`, `owner`, `class` (`read`, `write`, `ui`,
`kill`), `default: false`, and `removeBy` (ISO date). The optional `scope` field
accepts `workspace`; workspace-scoped entries are inventory-only in the v0 mobile
endpoint and return their defaults, independently of workspace configuration.
The initial 16 mobile flags belong to `mona` and retain legacy removal-date
metadata of `2027-01-31`. Removal eligibility follows the catalog kind below.

`tutoring_parent_message_v2` belongs to `pax`, defaults OFF, and has workspace
scope. Its runtime value comes from `workspace_configs`, independently of the
v0 mobile evaluator. Only the exact string `true` enables it; setting it to
`false` or removing it is the kill switch. See
[parent message v2](/platform/applications/tutoring#parent-message-v2).

## Add a flag

Name the flag in its PR, add its registry entry with default OFF, assign an owner
and lifecycle metadata, and wire its kill switch before enabling the feature.
Follow the
[trunk-based delivery rule](/build/development-tools/git-conventions#trunk-based-delivery):
flags default OFF; kill switch first, rollback second.

Run `cd packages/feature-flags && bun run generate` after editing the JSON, then
format the generated file with Oxc and commit it. `@tuturuuu/feature-flags`
exports `registry`, the generated `FlagKey` union, and the pure
`evaluateFlags(registry, context, overrides?)` function. Its tests validate the
registry and detect generated-source drift.

## When to add a flag

Gate new features behind a flag. Routine UX/UI changes and non-critical fixes ship
without one.

## Lifecycle catalog

`config/feature-flag-catalog.json` lists every platform flag family with its
lifecycle metadata. `@tuturuuu/feature-flags` exports it as `featureFlagCatalog`
together with `getFlagLifecycle` and `validateCatalog`.

| Family | Scope | Source of truth |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `mobile-runtime` | global | `config/feature-flags.json` and the mobile endpoint |
| `workspace-secret` | workspace | Workspace secrets read through `@tuturuuu/utils/feature-flags` and Infrastructure secret definitions |
| `mobile-build` | build | Non-secret mobile deployment settings compiled with `bool.fromEnvironment` |
| `runtime` | global | Store-backed rules with a legacy environment-variable fallback, evaluated by `evaluateRuntimeFlag` |

Each entry records `owner`, `createdAt`, `apps` (with `appsComplete` when every
consumer app is traced), `sources`, `defaults` per environment (`development`,
`staging`, `production`) and `verifiedOnProdAt`. Defaults are the declared value
when no override or workspace setting exists; they are not observed production
state.

`kind` separates removable feature flags from retained controls:

- `release` flags gate a new feature. Once `verifiedOnProdAt` is recorded,
  `removeBy` is derived as that instant plus 48 hours and the flag is overdue
  after it.
- `kill-switch`, `workspace-gate`, `safety-control` and `operational` entries are
  retained controls. Neither verification nor legacy deadline metadata makes them
  removal-due.

Entries adopted without historic metadata have `legacy: true`; their unknown owner
or creation date stays `null` and renders as unknown. For release flags only, a
`legacyRemoveBy` date is due through the end of that UTC day. New entries need
`legacy: false`, an owner,
`createdAt`, a description and a complete app list. Record `verifiedOnProdAt`
only from an actual production verification, never from defaults or CI results.

`packages/feature-flags/src/catalog.test.ts` fails when a source family gains or
loses a flag without a catalog change, when a recorded source stops naming its
flag, or when a new entry is marked legacy.

### Runtime flags

A `runtime` entry declares a `runtime` block next to its lifecycle metadata:

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `type` | `boolean`. |
| `scopes` | Rule scopes a stored rule may target: `platform` (required), `workspace`, `user`. |
| `controllers` | Who may set each scope. `platform` is always `platform-admin`. `workspace` is `platform-admin` (entitlements, rollouts) or `workspace-admin`. `user` is `platform-admin` (per-person overrides) or `self`. |
| `envFallback` | Legacy environment variable read only while no platform rule is stored, or `null`. `kill-switch` and `safety-control` flags must use `null`: they fall back to off only, because an unreachable store would otherwise let the environment enable a flag that has a stored kill rule. |
| `clientExposed` | Whether the evaluated boolean may reach a browser or app client. |
| `delegate` | Optional. `workspace` lets a workspace rule enable the flag on its own while the platform rule is `on` or absent. Requires the `workspace` scope. |

Runtime flags use the `global` scope and default to `false` in every
environment; validation rejects anything else. Every new feature that ships
dark registers one, so production can carry the code with the feature off.

`evaluateRuntimeFlag({ flag, context, rules, envValue })` is pure. The adapter
passes the verified actor (`userId`, `workspaceId`, `isStaff` from the server's
verified identity), the stored rules for the flag (or `null` when no snapshot is
available) and the raw environment value. Adapters pass lowercase UUIDs; the
evaluator also lowercases context, subject and allow-list ids before comparing,
and buckets rollouts on the lowercase ids. Only `null` means "no snapshot": any
other non-list value, including `undefined`, and any list holding a non-object
entry is a malformed snapshot and turns every flag off, as does a workspace or
user rule whose subject is not a UUID, since it names no subject to deny.

The platform rule is a **ceiling**. Precedence:

1. A malformed snapshot, a rule with an unknown scope, or a malformed or
   duplicated platform rule turns the flag off for everyone (`invalid-rules`).
   A malformed or duplicated workspace or user rule, or one for a scope the
   flag does not declare, turns the flag off only for its own subject; other
   workspaces and users are unaffected. Rules for other flags are ignored.
2. A platform `off` rule on a `kill-switch` flag turns it off (`kill-switch`).
3. While the platform rule is `off`, `staff` or `rollout`, a workspace or user
   rule can only narrow it: the result is the override's decision AND the
   platform decision. A workspace `on` under a platform `staff` rule is
   therefore staff-only.
4. One override decides inside that ceiling: a user rule for the actor when
   `controllers.user` is `platform-admin`, otherwise the workspace rule for the
   actor's workspace.
   - While the platform rule is `on` or absent, a `platform-admin` user rule
     decides alone (`on` or `off`).
   - A workspace rule decides alone only when the flag declares
     `delegate: 'workspace'` and the platform rule is `on` or absent. Without
     the delegate it narrows the environment fallback or the catalog default,
     so it cannot enable a flag that has no platform rule.
5. Without an override: the platform rule, then the environment fallback (only
   while no platform rule is stored; only the exact string `true` enables it,
   and it also applies when the snapshot is `null`), then the catalog default,
   which is off.

Only a stored platform `off` rule is a kill for every subject, including on a
`delegate: 'workspace'` flag; an environment fallback of `false` is not. A
`self` user rule can only turn an enabled result off; a user never grants a
feature to themselves. Per-person access beyond a platform `staff` or `rollout`
rule goes through that platform rule (`staff` mode or its allow-lists), not a
user rule.

Rule modes are `on`, `off`, `staff` (verified staff only) and `rollout`
(allow-listed workspaces or users, then a deterministic percentage bucket of
flag, user and workspace, so one user can land differently per workspace). Each
decision carries a `trace` of the steps taken.

Rule shape is shared by `ruleShapeError` in
`packages/feature-flags/src/rule-validation.ts`, the evaluator and the rule
store: a platform rule has a null subject and other scopes a UUID subject; a
user rule is `on` or `off`; a `rollout` rule has an integer percentage 0 to 100
and other modes none; allow-lists appear only on `rollout`, with at most 500
UUIDs each. `ruleMutationError` adds the write checks (operation id,
environment, reason, client, expected revision, and `self` rules limited to
`off` or unset) in the order the database applies them.

Cut a flag over to the store in two releases: store a platform rule equal to the
current environment value, then remove the environment variable and set
`envFallback` to `null`. The fallback still applies while the snapshot is
unavailable, so a stale environment variable must not outlive the cutover.
Requirements, because one malformed or duplicate rule turns the flag off for
everyone:

- Adapters must keep serving the last good snapshot instead of passing `null`
  once a flag has a stored platform rule.
- The write path must validate every rule with `ruleMutationError` before it
  calls the store, which rejects the same input again.

### Rule store

Migration `20261125030000_feature_flag_rules.sql` keeps runtime rules in the
`private` schema with the rule write RPC, and
`20261125030100_manage_feature_flags_permission.sql` adds the
`manage_feature_flags` root permission with the definition sync, read and
erasure RPCs. Migration `20261125080000_feature_flag_rules_hardening.sql`
preserves quota attribution across edits and indexes paging and audit lookups. Clients have no table access.

| Object | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `feature_flag_definitions` | The runtime block of each catalog runtime flag (`scopes`, `controllers`, `kind`, `delegate`). |
| `feature_flag_definition_audit` | Append-only receipt of each definition change, with the old and new definition and whether a control widening was acknowledged. |
| `feature_flag_rules` | One rule per flag, scope, subject and environment (`development` or `production`; there is no staging store). A null `mode` is an unset rule that keeps its revision. |
| `feature_flag_audit` | Append-only receipt per write: operation id, actor, old and new rule, old and new revision, `reason` (1 to 500 characters) and `client` (`admin-ui`, `workspace-ui`, `ttr`, `migration`, or `erasure` for subject erasure). |

The rule table's CHECK calls the same SQL shape function as the mutate RPC.
Triggers reject truncation, deletes, audit updates and any write outside the
RPC entrypoints; only the erasure entrypoint may delete rules and anonymize
audit rows. Every function pins `search_path = pg_catalog, pg_temp`. Only
`service_role` may execute the RPCs, and each RPC also refuses request claims
that name another role or no role; only a session with no request claims (a
direct database caller) is trusted without one.

**Definitions.** The admin app's server calls
`feature_flag_sync_definitions(p_definitions, p_acknowledge_widening)` with
`runtimeDefinitionRows(featureFlagCatalog.flags)`. The first
feature-flags dashboard or API read by a root flag manager starts one background
sync per admin process.
That sync uses `false` for widening and logs failures without blocking the read.
Root members with `manage_feature_flags` can trigger a sync or retry at
`POST /api/v1/infrastructure/feature-flags/sync`. The optional JSON field
`acknowledgeWidening` accepts a boolean and defaults to `false`. Cookie requests
need the feature-flags mutation header and same-origin intent. An unacknowledged
widening returns HTTP 409. An unchanged definition writes nothing, and each
change appends a definition audit row. It refuses malformed or duplicate definitions, a scope removal that
would orphan a live rule (`feature_flag_definition_orphans_rules`; unset those
rules first), and, unless `p_acknowledge_widening` is `true`, a change that
widens control over live rules (`feature_flag_definition_widens_control`):
moving a scope from `platform-admin` to `workspace-admin` or `self`, or newly
adding `delegate: 'workspace'` while workspace rules exist.

**Writes.** `feature_flag_mutate_rule(...)` validates the write, authorizes it
by the scope's controller, compares `p_expected_revision` (0 for a rule that
has never existed), and writes the rule and its audit row in one transaction:

- `platform-admin` requires the root permission `manage_feature_flags`; a
  tenant role holding the same permission name does not qualify.
- `workspace-admin` requires `manage_workspace_settings` in the subject
  workspace. Only that workspace's settings managers write a delegated
  workspace rule; root flag managers act through the platform ceiling and never
  edit a tenant's rule.
- `self` requires the actor to be the subject, and the mode may only be `off`
  or null. A null `p_mode` unsets the rule.
- A known `p_operation_id` replays its result only for the same actor and rule
  identity; otherwise the call fails with `feature_flag_operation_conflict`.
- Workspace and user rules that can enable a flag (any mode but `off`) are
  capped per flag and environment: 50000 in all (`feature_flag_rule_limit`)
  and, for a `workspace-admin` or `self` scope, 200 attributed to one actor
  (`feature_flag_actor_rule_limit`). Attribution goes to the actor who enables
  the rule and survives enabling-to-enabling edits. An `off` rule only narrows and is never
  capped, so self opt-outs and workspace kills keep working when a cap is
  full, and one tenant creating many workspaces cannot exhaust the shared
  cap. Platform-admin writes count toward the total but not the actor quota.
  Allow-lists hold at most 500 ids each.
- Every write holds the erasure lock in shared mode, and subject erasure holds
  it exclusively, so an erasure waits for in-flight writes and blocks new ones
  until it commits. A write committed after the erasure that still names the
  erased id (for example from a stale admin form) re-adds it. A repeated erasure removes any entry written later.
- The server sets `p_client` for its own surface; it never comes from a request
  body.

**Reads.** Evaluation combines two service-role reads:

- `feature_flag_read_snapshot(p_environment)` returns the live **platform**
  rules with a `version` digest. Cache it per isolate by version.
- `feature_flag_read_subject_rules(p_environment, p_workspace_id, p_user_id)`
  returns only the live workspace rules of the request's workspace and the
  user rules of its verified user, for a request-scoped lookup.

Pass both lists to `evaluateRuntimeFlag` as `rules`. If the subject read
fails, the adapter fails closed for that request (the flag is off) and never
evaluates with the snapshot alone, which would drop a workspace kill or a self
opt-out. Admin screens use `feature_flag_read_rules(p_actor, p_flag_key,
p_environment, p_limit, p_after_flag_key, p_after_scope, p_after_subject_id)`,
a page of 1 to 1000 rules (default 500) whose `nextCursor` is passed back as
the `p_after_*` arguments until it is null, and
`feature_flag_read_audit(p_actor, p_limit, p_before, p_before_id)`, which need
root `view_infrastructure` or `manage_feature_flags`; the audit pages newest
first on the `(occurredAt, id)` cursor of the last row.

**Control plane.** Platform admins write and read rules over
`/api/v1/infrastructure/feature-flags/rules` and its `/audit` route, with the
actor and client taken from the session; the contract is `parseRuleWrite` and
`ruleWriteResponse` in `packages/feature-flags/src/rule-api.ts`. The `ttr flags`
command group wraps it, see [feature flags CLI](/reference/packages/cli-feature-flags).

**Deferred erasure.** Migration `20261125085000_feature_flag_erasure_intents.sql`
records one row in `private.feature_flag_erasure_intents` after every delete on
`auth.users` and `public.workspaces`. The trigger does constant work: it never
takes the erasure lock or reads the rule store, so account and workspace
deletes stay cheap. A drain (service role) works the queue in bounded steps:

- `feature_flag_erasure_claim(p_limit)` leases 1 to 20 due intents. The lease is
  `next_attempt_at`, pushed out by 2^attempts minutes (at most an hour), so a
  stalled worker's claim returns by itself and a failing subject backs off.
- `feature_flag_erasure_complete(p_id)` runs `feature_flag_erase_subject` and
  deletes the intent in one transaction. A wait on the erasure lock longer than
  the lock timeout (`55P03`) rolls the erasure back, records `lock_not_available`
  on the intent and returns `busy`; an unknown id returns `gone`.
- `feature_flag_erasure_status()` reports pending and due counts, the highest
  attempt count and the oldest intent, for the drain's stop fence and alerts.

While an intent is pending, `feature_flag_mutate_rule` refuses a write whose
subject, or whose allow-list entry, names that user or workspace
(`feature_flag_subject_erasing`). Rules of a deleted subject stay stored, inert
at evaluation, and keep counting toward the 50000-rule cap until the drain
reaches them. Until the Cloudflare job that runs the drain is deployed, intents
accumulate and erasure stays a manual `feature_flag_erase_subject` call.

See the
[data protection standard](/platform/data-protection-standard#runtime-feature-flag-rules).

**Rollback.** Roll back the erasure intents migration first; its rollback restores the hardening `feature_flag_mutate_rule` and drops the queue, triggers and drain RPCs. Then roll back the hardening migration to remove its indexes
and quota attribution. The `manage_feature_flags` enum value
cannot be removed. Its rollback drops the definition sync, read and erasure RPCs. The rule store rollback drops
every rule and audit row, so export `private.feature_flag_audit` and
`private.feature_flag_definition_audit` first.

Regression coverage is in
`packages/feature-flags/src/rule-store-contract.test.ts`, which binds each shape
case to the same named case in
`apps/database/supabase/tests/feature-flag-rule-store.sql`, and
`runtime-ceiling.test.ts` for subject-scoped invalid rules.

Dependencies between flags stay with the caller: for example
`MEET_FORMS_EXTENDED_ENABLED` also requires `MEET_FORMS_ENABLED`. Runtime
`kill-switch` flags default off like every runtime flag, so they guard features
that ship dark. The Infrastructure dashboard lists runtime entries read-only
until the rule store accepts them.

Regression coverage is in `packages/feature-flags/src/runtime-evaluate.test.ts`,
`runtime-ceiling.test.ts` and `catalog.test.ts`.

### Overdue check

`node packages/feature-flags/scripts/check-lifecycle.mjs` reports malformed
metadata and overdue flags as GitHub annotations. Cheap PR Checks runs it in
warning mode, which exits 0. `--strict` exits 1 on any report; `--now <iso>` and
`--catalog <path>` pin the clock and input.

### Dashboard

Infrastructure `/<wsId>/feature-flags` renders every catalog flag for root
workspace members with `view_infrastructure`. A root member with
`manage_workspace_roles` can override the 16 mobile-runtime registry keys per
`development`, `staging`, and `production`. The page shows the declared default
and the effective value after the `mobile_offline` master gate. Workspace-secret
flags stay read-only, with the label "Managed per workspace in Secrets" and a
link to `/<wsId>/workspaces`. Mobile-build flags stay read-only and are labeled
build-time. `cookieConsentBanner` is a separate export and is not a registry
toggle. Saved-state or audit failure stays explicit. The page does not invent a
persisted OFF value, and it does not select a workspace or write workspace
secrets.

Platform state is one row per flag key and environment. Resetting to the declared
default keeps the revision and stores an empty override. Audit is append-only.
Merging this documentation does not apply the database migration or expose the
private functions; that deployment is separate.

### Server and Worker readers

In framework-free server code, create a module-level `createRuntimeReader` with
an injected private service-role RPC function and a server environment reader
(`readEnv`). Call `evaluateFlag(key, context)` for one decision or
`evaluateFlags(keys, context)` for a map of decisions. Pass the deployment
environment, verified `userId`, verified `workspaceId` and verified `isStaff`.
A batch makes one subject RPC for its request. Subject results stay in that
evaluation. In Web, use
`isFeatureEnabled(key, { request, workspaceId })` from
`@/lib/feature-flags/server`; omit `request` in a server component to use the web
session. Web resolves the actor and verifies membership in the supplied workspace
before fetching rules. Feature evaluation supplements the feature's existing
permission checks.

The platform snapshot is single-flight per store environment and refreshed on
demand after 60 seconds. Each server RPC has a two-second deadline. Transport failures can reuse the last validated
snapshot until it reaches 10 minutes old. A malformed response fails closed.
After expiry, a known stored platform rule stays off even if a legacy env var
still says `true`. An uncached or absent platform rule can use only the
catalog's declared fallback. Staging has no store. Requests that need subject
rules fail closed when those rules cannot be read.

The Worker snapshot endpoint is
`GET /api/v1/feature-flags/snapshot?environment=production|development`.
Set `FEATURE_FLAGS_SNAPSHOT_TOKEN` in Web and in the calling Worker's server
bindings and send it as a bearer credential. Use a randomly generated opaque
credential with an `ff_snapshot_` prefix so provider auth middleware classifies
it as a service credential. The response contains only platform rule data
(including any rollout allow-lists), is private and non-cacheable in intermediaries,
and carries a strong ETag. The endpoint validates the current store response before
returning 304.

Create one module-level `createRemoteRuntimeReader({ environment, env })` per
Worker isolate. Set `FEATURE_FLAGS_SNAPSHOT_URL` to the full endpoint URL and
pass the Worker bindings as `env`. The Worker uses HTTPS outside loopback,
does not follow redirects, and sends `If-None-Match` for the last validated ETag.
A 304 renews the age of that snapshot. Worker evaluation uses platform rules
for context where only the platform rule can apply. If the supplied workspace
or user would need a subject rule, the Worker returns off. Use the server
reader for those decisions.

Each isolate makes at most one subrequest per rolling 60 seconds, shared by
concurrent evaluations. The request and response body have a combined two-second
deadline. A subsequent demand can retry in the next 60-second slot. There are
no background retries or timers between requests. A fresh isolate starts with
one eligible read. Set `FEATURE_FLAGS_REMOTE=off` in the Worker bindings to
stop subrequests even after a restart. Missing URL or token also disables
transport. These configurations use the catalog fallback for eligible flags.
The shared stale bound is 10 minutes after the last validated snapshot.
`runtime-remote.test.ts` covers request counts under bursts, 304 reuse, deadlines,
stale expiry, cold starts, scoped denial and the stop switch.

## Mobile endpoint

`GET /api/v1/mobile/feature-flags?wsId=<uuid>` accepts the existing session or
mobile app-session authentication. Authentication failures return 401. `wsId` is
optional; when supplied it must be a UUID (400 otherwise), and the caller must
belong to that workspace (403 otherwise). Membership lookup failures return 500.

A 200 response contains only:

```json
{
  "version": "<sha256>",
  "ttlSeconds": 30,
  "flags": { "mobile_offline": false, "offline_read_notes": false }
}
```

The example abbreviates `flags`; the response includes **every registry key**.
`version` hashes the JSON payload `{ttlSeconds, flags}` with SHA-256, excluding
`version` itself. `ETag` is that version in double quotes. A matching
`If-None-Match` returns 304 with no body, after authentication and membership
checks. Responses use `Cache-Control: private, no-cache` and
`Vary: Authorization, Cookie`. The mobile reader polls using the 30-second TTL
and retains the last payload on 304. No user or workspace identifiers are
returned. User identity comes only from the authenticated session; query
parameters cannot select a user. The handler uses
`await connection()` for request-time evaluation, with no shared output cache.
Both `CDN-Cache-Control` and `Vercel-CDN-Cache-Control` are `no-store`, including
304 and error responses.

## Evaluation

After authentication and membership, the endpoint reads platform overrides for
one server-selected environment. `VERCEL_ENV=production` selects production,
`preview` selects staging, and `development` selects development. An unknown
`VERCEL_ENV` selects production. When `VERCEL_ENV` is unset, `NODE_ENV` of
`development` or `test` selects development and every other value selects
production. A query or body field cannot select the environment.

Missing or unreachable storage uses each registry default. An authorization
failure or a malformed payload returns an error and does not substitute defaults.
The pure evaluator accepts overrides for known keys only and applies the kill
switch last: `mobile_offline: false` forces every `offline_` key OFF, including
reads, writes and status UI. Context currently has no effect on the boolean
result. This endpoint does not enable offline functionality or grant access to
underlying data.

Regression coverage lives in `packages/feature-flags/src/index.test.ts`,
`packages/feature-flags/src/{catalog,lifecycle,check-lifecycle}.test.ts`,
`apps/web/src/app/api/v1/mobile/feature-flags/route.test.ts` and the Infrastructure
`feature-flags` page and table tests.

Cookie-authenticated state mutations require the Infrastructure origin and the
`x-tuturuuu-feature-flag-action: 1` header. Bearer API requests use verified token
authentication without a cookie fallback.

## Server-side audience rules

New release flags declare rollout metadata in the central catalog: stage,
owner and a calendar-date removal deadline. Stages are internal, rollout and ga.
Internal audiences default to the exact tuturuuu.com email domain. Subdomains,
suffix matches, anonymous identities, missing emails and unconfirmed emails are
denied. Server adapters pass an actor returned by verified authentication,
including email_confirmed_at. Request JSON, query parameters, editable profile
metadata and a badge never establish that identity.

Call isFeatureEnabled(key, { user, workspace, permissionGranted }, configuration)
on the server before rendering a surface or performing its operation.
The enabledFlags configuration contains the owning evaluator's boolean results,
including its kill-switch rules. The rollouts configuration contains reviewed
catalog policies. Missing policies fail closed. The caller passes its existing
authorization result as permissionGranted; an audience never grants access.
Do not cache the result across actors or workspaces or trust a client suffix check.

An internal policy can declare emailDomainAllowlist; an empty list admits nobody.
Rollout policies select explicit workspace IDs or an integer percentage from
0 to 100. Percentage assignment is deterministic for the flag, actor and workspace;
it is a rollout decision, not a security boundary. GA retains flag and permission
gates until the owning source unit removes the flag after production verification.

The Infrastructure inventory shows configured stages, owners and removal
deadlines. Adopted entries without rollout metadata remain explicitly unknown;
the inventory does not invent verification or ownership. The existing mobile
boolean evaluator and its 16-key response remain unchanged. Each surface adopts
server-side audience enforcement in its owning source unit; a catalog policy
does not retrofit client-only or build-time consumers. Workspace-secret and
mobile-build entries remain read-only.

Regression coverage is in packages/feature-flags/src/audience.test.ts and the
Infrastructure read-model tests. Source-declared policies require no database
migration or separate global badge flag.
